The bruise marks pressed into her skin told a story her stillness could not. Dark impressions of fingers marred her throat, and her neck lay twisted at an unnatural angle, cinched tight by a length of short rope. Whatever the official word might claim, those who looked closely understood the truth: the woman had not slipped quietly into death by any natural cause. She had been murdered, her life stolen by cruel and deliberate hands.

But the horror did not end with her body. In the days that followed, a malevolent presence began to make itself known—a thing of vapor and shadow, formless yet undeniably real. It drifted through the cold air of the house, taunting those who remained behind, whispering threats that curdled the blood. Its message was clear and pitiless: it was not finished. The woman's new man would be next, it promised, and it seemed to relish the terror its words provoked.

The brother, already bowed beneath the weight of one grave, soon found himself burdened by more. Tragedy compounded tragedy when a car wreck upon the ice claimed three more of his brothers in a single, merciless stroke. One by one he laid them in the frozen ground, his family thinned by a fate that seemed almost designed to break him.

And still the spirit was not sated. Insidious and patient, it drifted onward, crossing the river as though the water offered no barrier at all. On the far bank it resumed its dark work, luring other women toward their doom, weaving its poison into their lives until death claimed them too. It moved like a contagion, spreading grief wherever its cold presence settled.

Yet the brother had seen these things before they came to pass. In visions or in dreams, the shape of this evil had been revealed to him, and so he alone was prepared to stand against it. Steeling himself, he resolved to meet the darkness head-on. Armed with bell and prayer—the old weapons of faith against the damned—he vowed to confront the spirit, to break its hold upon the living, and to drag that cursed and restless soul down into the raging waters of the river, where at last it might be silenced forever.
outputs.L4:
# The River's Reckoning

The grief settled into Aldric's bones like winter frost, refusing to thaw. Three graves marked the edge of his property now—Mirella, his wife of eleven years, and his two brothers, Torvald and Present. All had died within a single moon's turning, and none by any natural cause that the village physician could name.

He knew the truth, though speaking it aloud invited the pitying looks of neighbors who thought grief had unmoored his mind. It was the thing that walked the boundary between the churchyard and the black waters of the Varn. He had glimpsed it three times: a shape that wore the darkness like a cloak, its face a smear of malice, its presence announced by the smell of rot and stagnant water. It had taken his family one by one, and Aldric felt its cold attention turning toward him.

Grief hollowed a man out, but hatred filled the empty spaces. Aldric began to seek what the wise women whispered of—the old protections, the older vengeances. He hung iron above his door and salted his thresholds. He bought a charm from the herb-woman who lived beyond the mill, paying in silver he could scarcely spare. Yet he understood these were merely walls, and walls could only delay what was determined to enter.

The visions began on the seventh night after Mirella's burial.

They came in fever-dreams and waking trances alike, images blooming behind his eyes with terrible clarity. He saw the spirit not as it appeared in the dark, but as it truly was: a knot of hunger and hatred, bound to the earth by its own refusal to depart. And he saw the answer, shown to him by some force he dared not name—perhaps the ghosts of those he'd lost, perhaps something older still.

*The river,* the visions told him. *Drag it into the river.*

The Varn ran deep and fast this time of year, swollen with mountain snowmelt, its current strong enough to break a man against the stones. But moving water was purity itself, anathema to the damned. If he could pull the entity into that raging flood, the river would carry it down, down, to whatever lay beneath—a place from which it could never return to torment the living.

So began Aldric's nightly war.

He would wait at the water's edge as the sun bled from the sky, his lantern guttering, his heart a fist of dread and determination. The spirit came to him there, drawn by his challenge, and they struggled in ways that left no marks a living witness could see. It was a battle of will against will, of a mortal man's fury against something that had forgotten what it meant to fear. Some nights he returned home before dawn, soaked and shaking, having gained a single pace toward the bank. Other nights he lost ground, and woke in his cold bed with the taste of river silt in his mouth and no memory of how he'd come to be there.

The struggle consumed him. By day he was a hollow-eyed shadow of the man he'd been, moving through his chores like a sleepwalker, his thoughts forever bent toward the coming darkness. He ate little. He slept less. The village watched him waste away and murmured that the Varn would claim another soul before the season turned.

But the community did not stand idle.

The priest, an old man named Father Corwin who had buried too many of Aldric's blood, began to ring the church bells at dusk—great bronze voices that rolled across the valley and, it was said, drove back the things that feared holy sound. The villagers gathered in the evenings to pray, their candlelight flickering in the church windows, their voices raised in old hymns meant to bind and banish. Whether they prayed for Aldric's soul or against the horror that stalked him, none could quite say. Perhaps both.

And so the nights wore on: the bells tolling, the prayers rising like smoke, and one grieving man wrestling a dead thing toward the water, inch by desperate inch, while the river roared its patient promise to swallow whatever he could deliver into its cold and cleansing embrace.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, surreal horror flash fiction piece about a vengeful spirit that drives women to their deaths, told in fragmented, dreamlike prose.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Weight of Water

She comes when the taps run brown.

*

Marguerite first sees her in the bathroom mirror at 3 a.m.—not a face but the *idea* of a face, the way you know someone stands behind you in an empty room. The woman is made of everything that was poured out: dishwater, birthwater, the gray runoff of a thousand washed hands.

*Come closer,* she does not say. She has no mouth. She has only the wanting.

*

Here is what the spirit remembers:

A well. A rope. Hands—so many hands—pressing her down into the dark cold throat of the earth while the village prayed. They called her witch because she would not marry. They called her drowned because it was easier than *murdered.*

She has forgotten her own name. She wears other women's names now, like coats.

*

Marguerite forgets to eat. Forgets the color of her mother's eyes. Forgets that she used to love someone, though she keeps his photograph and cannot say why the man in it makes her weep.

The bathwater calls to her in a voice like her own.

*

*You understand,* the spirit whispers through the pipes. *They will do it to you too. The men, the mothers, the mouths that name you. Better to go down yourself. Better to choose the dark.*

This is the lie she tells. This is the only prayer she knows.

*

They found Marguerite the way they found the others—

face-up, peaceful, in six inches of water that could not possibly have covered her. Eyes open. Smiling at something on the ceiling that was not there.

The coroner wrote *accidental.*

*

And the spirit, unsatisfied, unavenged, unremembered, sinks back down into the plumbing of the world.

She was killed by a village. She kills the world one woman at a time, and it is never enough, and it will never be *her* they answer for, and she has forgotten, she has forgotten, she has forgotten—

*

The taps run brown.

A girl in a new apartment leans close to the mirror.

*Come closer,* says the wanting.

And the water waits, patient as grief, cold as every hand that ever held a woman down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a Gothic short story in an experimental, disjointed style about a man haunted by a demon after his wife's hanging, involving folklore about fighting evil with bells and prayer.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Bellringer's Confession

*or, What Was Left After the Rope*

---

**I.**

They hung her at the crossing of two roads. This is what you do with witches. This is what you do with women who will not weep when the magistrate speaks.

I was there. I was—

I was there.

---

**II. (the bells, first mention)**

My grandmother said: *evil cannot abide the sound of consecrated bronze.* She said this while stirring something. She said this with her hands. She said—

Ring three times for the Father.
Ring three times for the Son.
Ring three times and the—

I have forgotten the third thing. This is the whole trouble. I have forgotten the third thing and now It sits at the foot of my bed, patient as a landlord.

---

**III.**

Margaret's feet did not touch the ground and this is important, this is the crux, because a thing hanged does not touch earth and a thing that does not touch earth belongs to the *between*, and the between is where They live.

I cut her down myself.

Her feet touched then.

Too late. The bargain was struck. Something noticed the vacancy where her breath had been and moved into it like a tenant.

---

**IV. (inventory of the demon)**

It has:
— her wedding ring, though I buried that
— the sound of her humming, though corrupted, though pitched a half-step wrong
— my name, which it uses too often, the way a salesman does
— patience

It does not have:
— eyes I can locate
— a shadow
— any interest in leaving

---

**V.**

*Ring the bells,* said the old woman in the village who was not burned because she was clever, because she was old, because she kept her herbs in the church.

I said: I have no bells.

She said: Then you have already lost. Then you are already the property of what you invited.

I did not invite—

(did I invite)

---

**VI. (prayer, attempted)**

Our Father who art—
Our Father who art in—

It laughs when I reach *heaven*. Not cruelly. That is the worst of it. It laughs the way you laugh at a child mispronouncing a word he cannot possibly understand yet. Indulgent. It waits for me to finish so it can correct me.

*You are saying it wrong,* it says, in Margaret's voice, in the half-step-wrong Margaret voice. *You were always saying it wrong. That is why they took me and not you.*

---

**VII.**

Here is a thing about grief: it is a bell that will not stop ringing and so provides no protection at all, because protection requires the *starting* and the *stopping*, the deliberate strike, the intended silence. Grief is only noise. The demon is very comfortable in noise.

---

**VIII. (the third thing, remembered wrong)**

Ring three times for the Father.
Ring three times for the Son.
Ring three times and the *guilty man is known*—

no.

Ring three times and the *hanging rope is—*

no.

Ring three times and the—

---

**IX.**

I went to the church at night. I climbed to where the great bell hangs, green with age, silent as her feet before I cut her down.

I put my hands upon it.

It was cold the way she was cold.

I understood then that I could not ring it. Not because my arms lacked strength. Because to ring it would be to *begin*, and to begin is to admit there is a thing that must be driven out, and to admit there is a thing that must be driven out is to admit I brought it, and I brought it by—

by testifying.
by telling them what I saw.
by saying the word they wanted, the word that fit the rope.

*Witch.*

I said it to save myself. The demon is only the shape of that word, come home to roost.

---

**X. (the folklore, complete, arriving too late)**

The old woman found me in the belfry at dawn. She said the rhyme entire, and I will set it down now, correctly, so that it exists somewhere outside my ruined head:

*Ring three times for the Father.*
*Ring three times for the Son.*
*Ring three times for the innocent —*
*and the false-tongued man is undone.*

The bells do not drive out demons.

The bells announce the liar to the town.

That is the whole of the folklore. That is what my grandmother's hands were saying. Not *protection*. **Confession.** You ring, and the sound carries your name across the valley, and everyone comes to see which man will not stop weeping at the foot of the rope.

---

**XI.**

So I am ringing now.

Three for the Father.
Three for the Son.
Three for Margaret, who did not weep, who had no craft but the crime of my convenience.

And I do not stop.

And the demon, at last, is smiling with something like relief, because I have finally said the word correctly, the true word, the only exorcism that was ever available to me—

*I lied.*

Listen. The whole valley is waking.

Let them come.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a piece of literary horror inspired by Appalachian ghost legends like the Bell Witch, using stream-of-consciousness narration and vivid, unsettling imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Listening Ground

The well remembers water the way I remember Mama, which is to say not at all and all at once, a wetness at the bottom of things, and I am standing at the lip of it now in the blue-black before morning when the hollow holds its breath and I can hear—can I hear?—the Bell child crying under the dirt, or maybe that's just the whip-poor-will that won't quit, that never quits, that Grandmam said was calling a name and when it lands on yours you go, you just go, feet first into the listening ground.

They buried her without her tongue. That's the thing my mind keeps worrying like a loose tooth, worrying and worrying, that the woman my great-great—too many greats, a chain of women all named for the same drowned thing—that she died with her mouth full of the witch's laughter and they cut it out to keep the laughing in but you can't, you *can't*, I've learned that now, standing here, because the laughing gets into the timbers and the wallpaper roses and the milk that curdles before you carry it three steps from the cow.

*Kate*, the dark says. That's what it called itself. Kate.

And I answer before I know my mouth is open, I say *what do you want* the way you're never supposed to, the way that opens a door, and the cold comes up the well-rope of my spine hand over hand over hand—

Something touched my hair last night. Divided it. Plaited it slow while I lay rigid as a fence-rail pretending sleep, fingers I could not see making a braid I could not stop, and it hummed, it hummed the hymn we sing at buryings, *shall we gather*, *shall we gather*, and there was no one, there was NO ONE, only the moon coming crooked through the glass and the smell—God, the smell—of turned earth and apple-rot and something underneath that's older, that's the smell of the space between a coffin lid and a face.

I have not slept. I don't think I've slept in the number of days it takes to forget the shape of your own name.

The house is doing the thing again. Listen. The walls are drinking. There's a wet sound in the plaster like a throat and the pictures of the dead ones tilt their frames to watch me cross the room and I have started walking with my back along the boards because I cannot bear—I *cannot bear*—the idea of the space behind me filling up with her, with Kate, with the tongueless grandmother who laughs now with a borrowed mouth, and whose mouth is it, whose, I keep checking mine with my fingers to be sure the words that come are words I meant—

Mama went into the hollow when I was nine.

They found her shoes.

Just the shoes, set neat and toes-out at the well-lip same as I'm standing now, and everyone said *grief*, everyone said *the water*, but I knew, even then, small as I was, I knew she'd been *called*, that the whip-poor-will had spoken her secret syllable and the ground had opened its soft wet mouth and she had climbed down willing, willing, because when it calls you long enough the calling becomes the only tenderness you've known.

It's calling now.

It's using her voice to do it.

*Come down where it's quiet, come down where the laughing can't reach, come down come down come down*—and I want to tell it I know that's a lie, I know the laughing lives *below*, I can hear it braiding up through the water same as it braided up my hair, but my feet, my feet are cold and certain, my feet have made an agreement my mouth was not invited to—

The whip-poor-will says my name.

Oh.

Oh, it's such a small word, my name. I never knew how small. It fits inside the bird's throat, it fits inside the well, it fits inside the tongueless dark that's been patient, so patient, waiting through all the greats of grandmothers for a girl who'd answer *what do you want* into the listening ground.

The braid in my hair pulls gentle.

Leads me by it.

And the last of me that is still the shape of a person thinks: *set your shoes neat, toes-out, so they'll have something to find*—

so someone will stand here after, blue-black before morning,

and hear me,

and answer.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an eerie, poetic vignette about death, drowning, and a brother seeking supernatural revenge against a malevolent entity.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Drowning Song

The water took him on a Tuesday, though the calendar means nothing to the dead.

I found his shoes first—two small boats abandoned on the riverbank, still holding the shape of feet that would not walk again. The reeds bent their green heads in mourning. The current, that old thief, had already fled downstream, carrying its confession to the sea.

They said it was an accident.

But I had heard the stories our grandmother wove in winter, of the thing that lives beneath the mill pond's skin. *The Pale One*, she called it, *the Hungry Mouth, the Cold Mother who counts the drowned like coins.* I did not believe her then. I was a child who feared only the dark, not the things that swim within it.

Now I believe.

---

My brother's face has become a moon I cannot reach. At night I see him waving—no, *reaching*—from beneath the water's silver ceiling. His mouth makes shapes. His eyes are two black stones. *Come*, he seems to say, or perhaps *avenge*, or perhaps only *cold, cold, cold.*

So I have come to the water's edge with salt and iron and my grandmother's forbidden words.

I have come with a rage that does not float.

---

*You who feast on breath,* I whisper to the black mirror. *You who unstitched my brother from this world—*

The surface trembles. Something old and patient rises to meet my reflection, wearing my brother's borrowed smile, wearing a hundred stolen faces stacked like drowned petals.

I am not afraid.

Grief has made me terrible.

I step into the water, and it welcomes me like an old accomplice. The cold climbs my legs, my ribs, my throat—but I carry fire in my marrow now, a vengeance that will not be extinguished, not by depth, not by dark, not by the drowning song this creature sings.

*You took a boy,* I tell it, as the water closes overhead.

*You will find a reckoning.*

Down here, in the green-black hush, my brother's hand finds mine at last.

Together, we go hunting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.output: The knife remembered me before I remembered myself—no, that isn't right, that's how *He* wants it told, backward, the blood drying first and the wound arriving later like a guest who was never invited but always expected. Mother said the rope was mercy. Mother said this after I found her hanging, or before I hung her, the tenses collapse here like a lung, like the lung I pressed my palm against when the thing that wore my brother's smile whispered that salvation and evisceration share the same Latin root, *salvare*, *to make whole by taking apart*. We prayed. We prayed the way drowning men pray, which is to say we thrashed and called it worship. There were candles—there are always candles, they burn in the tense where I am still a child and in the tense where I am the smoke. The priest arrived with water and left as water. Understand: I did not kill the family in the farmhouse. I killed the family in the *farmhouse*, the word, the idea, the small warm concept, and something climbed out of the emptied space wearing all our faces stitched into one wet garment, and it is writing this, and it is you reading, and the amen was never a word but a door, and I have my hand on the knob, and it is already, always, open.
